description: Process creation, termination, and service installation events from the Windows Security log.

source.note: 4688 requires 'Audit Process Creation' to be enabled. Command-line capture requires an additional policy ('Include command line in process creation events').

4688.headline: A new process was started
4688.plain_english: A program was started. If you don't recognize the program, or if it was launched by a suspicious parent (like Office launching PowerShell), investigate.
4688.technical_description: Security event 4688: a new process was created. Key fields: NewProcessName, CreatorProcessName (parent), CommandLine (if enabled), SubjectUserName, TokenElevationType.
4688.when: Time Windows recorded the process creation.
4688.why_it_matters: Process creation shows what actually ran — the parent-child relationship is often more useful than the child alone.
suspicious_when: Office apps (winword.exe, excel.exe) spawning powershell.exe, cmd.exe, or wscript.exe
Processes running from %TEMP%, %APPDATA%, Downloads, or C:\Users\Public
Unexpected parent process (e.g. services.exe spawning cmd.exe)
Command lines with encoded or obfuscated arguments
what_to_do: Check the parent process and command line
Verify the executable path is legitimate (not a user-writable folder)
Correlate with 4624 for the account and 4689 for exit

severity.low: Known app launched by expected parent
severity.high: Office/browser spawning interpreters (PowerShell, cmd, wscript) or execution from user-writable paths

4688.important_note: Command line, if captured, is one of the most useful fields — enable it if the audit policy allows.

4689.headline: A process stopped
4689.plain_english: A program stopped running. Usually routine — correlate with 4688 to know how long it ran and how it exited.
4689.technical_description: Security event 4689: a process exited. Status field indicates exit code.
4689.why_it_matters: Exit code can show whether a process crashed, was terminated, or completed normally.
suspicious_when: Process exited with an unexpected error
what_to_do: Correlate with the matching 4688 by PID

severity.high: Process termination that correlates with suspicious activity

4689.important_note: Low-signal on its own — use with 4688.

4697.headline: A service was installed
4697.plain_english: A new Windows service (a background program) was installed. Attackers use services to run malicious code persistently. If you didn't install a new service, investigate.
4697.technical_description: Security event 4697: a service was installed. Key fields: ServiceName, ServiceFileName, ServiceType, ServiceStartType, ServiceAccount.

where.Computer: Machine where the service was installed

4697.why_it_matters: Services are a persistence mechanism — the binary path and account are key.
suspicious_when: Service binary in a user-writable folder (%TEMP%, %APPDATA%)
Service account is LocalSystem but binary path is unusual
Service installed outside a documented change window
Service name mimics a Windows service
what_to_do: Check the binary path — is it a legitimate location?
Correlate with 4688 for the process that installed the service
If unauthorized, disable the service and investigate

severity.high: Service binary from user-writable path, or install correlated with other suspicious activity

4697.important_note: Also correlate with System-log event 7045 ('A service was installed in the system').

implementation_notes.verified_field: Only display a plain-English explanation when `verified` is true.
implementation_notes.sysmon_note: Sysmon events (1, 3, 5, 11, 13, 22, etc.) belong to the Microsoft-Windows-Sysmon/Operational channel, not the Security log. Add a separate sysmon.json if Sysmon is installed.
